binders: p is an arbitrary sequence indexed by natural numbers, with each p(n) a real number in the closed interval [0,1].
C is an arbitrary real number.
hypotheses: Eventually as n tends to infinity through the natural numbers, (n-1) p(n) <= C, where n-1 is natural-number subtraction and is then cast to a real.
conclusions: Eventually as n tends to infinity, under the binomial random simple-graph law on vertex set Fin n with edge parameter p(n), the real measure of the event that every vertex v has degree strictly less than ((C+5) log n)/(log(log n)) is at least 9/10.
mathematical_definitions: Eventually atTop on Nat means: there exists N such that the asserted property holds for every natural n >= N.
The binomial random graph law is the measure obtained from Bernoulli edge choices of parameter p(n) on unordered pairs of distinct vertices of Fin n.
The degree of v in G is the cardinality of the set of vertices adjacent to v.
The measured event is {G : SimpleGraph (Fin n) | for every v in Fin n, degree_G(v) < ((C+5) log(n))/(log(log(n)))}.
Measure.real converts the measure's extended-nonnegative-real value of this event to a real number before comparison with 9/10.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every sequence of edge probabilities p(n) in [0,1] and every nonnegative real C, if (n-1)p(n) is at most C for all sufficiently large n, then for all sufficiently large n a binomial random simple graph on n labeled vertices with edge probability p(n) has, with probability at least 0.9, every vertex degree strictly below (C+5) log(n) / log(log(n)).

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The edge probability is allowed to depend arbitrarily on n; the only asymptotic restriction is the eventual upper bound (n-1)p(n) <= C.
Both the bound assumption and the probability conclusion are eventual statements, and their cutoffs need not be the same before combining them.
The theorem assumes C >= 0 even though the eventual bound and p(n) >= 0 already constrain which negative C could occur.
The degree inequality is strict (<), not <=, even though degree is natural-valued and the threshold is real-valued.
Natural subtraction makes n-1 equal to 0 at n=0; this exceptional value is harmless to an eventual assertion but is part of the literal formal statement.

Real.log is totalized: log(0)=0 and for nonzero negative inputs it uses the absolute value; real division is also totalized at denominator 0. Thus the displayed threshold has a formal value even for exceptional small n, although eventuality permits discarding all such n.
For n=0, the universal assertion over v : Fin 0 is vacuous; eventuality again permits this isolated case to be irrelevant.
The conclusion asserts only the fixed lower bound 9/10, not convergence of the probability to 1.
The target does not explicitly state edge independence or an elementary probability formula; those semantics enter through the definition of the binomial-random-graph measure.
Measure.real uses an extended-real-to-real conversion; no explicit finiteness premise is stated in the target, though the selected graph law is a probability measure.
ambiguities: The dossier gives LocalDef004 only as an inductive type and does not display its field names or eliminator, but its constructor, projections, and LocalDef003 body determine the two components relevant to this proposition.

The one-level definition of the binomial graph law exposes a Bernoulli measure on unordered non-loop pairs but does not expand the deeper semantics of ProbabilityTheory.setBernoulli; the standard independent-edge interpretation is therefore mediated by that named dependency beyond the displayed semantic frontier.
